title: Goldman private credit fund defies industry elevated withdrawal trend again yet again - WKZO
content: Sept 29 (Reuters) – Goldman Sachs’ private credit fund said on Tuesday that investor requests to pull money further slowed down ​in the third-quarter tender offer, with redemption pressure easing ‌across the broader industry. The $18.2 billion GS Credit fund once again outperformed most other private credit players, with investors seeking to pull just 2% of shares in the latest tender offer, compared with 3.2% in the ‌prior ​quarter. Its repurchase requests have remained ⁠below the customary 5% ⁠limit since inception. Meanwhile, withdrawal requests at the biggest non-traded private credit funds have ranged from 10% to over 16% of shares in the third-quarter tender offers unveiled so far. ​Data from Blue Owl funds is expected in the coming days. Rival funds have grappled with elevated redemption requests throughout ⁠2026, driven by concerns about ⁠lending standards and whether software companies that have ​borrowed heavily from direct lenders will weather AI disruption. That said, redemption ​pressure at major funds is showing signs of ‌easing as asset managers clear backlogs of withdrawal requests and investor sentiment rebounds from recent turbulence. A huge chunk of GS Credit investors come from Goldman’s private wealth channels, who have been ⁠long-term investors in the private credit space and can tolerate illiquidity, Reuters has reported. “The concerns around software-related credit quality that dominated ⁠headlines earlier in ‌2026 have begun to moderate. While Q1’s “SaaSpocalypse” narrative ⁠and Q2’s enterprise software spend uncertainty drove ​aggressive ‌spread widening, the Q3 landscape has shifted meaningfully,” ​GS Credit ⁠said. On the subscriptions side, GS Credit said it generated roughly $400 million of gross inflows during the quarter. Its Class I shares have delivered a roughly 9.4% total return since inception through August 31, 2026. (Reporting by Arasu Kannagi Basil in Bengaluru; Editing ​by Vijay Kishore)

title: 8K-Mile 1989 Nissan 300ZX GS 5-Speed Is a Blue-on-Blue One-Owner Time Capsule - Motorious
content: Classic car news, hand-picked vehicles, and auction coverage. Choose what lands in your inbox. Some cars get parked because they're broken. Others get parked because someone loved them too much to use them up. This 1989 Nissan 300ZX GS clearly falls into the second camp. Currently listed on Hagerty Marketplace, the Bright Blue Metallic coupe shows just 7,700 miles, wears its original-owner story proudly, and still pairs Nissan's smooth VG30E V6 with the five-speed manual that makes a Z31 so much fun to drive. The Z31-generation 300ZX arrived for 1984 and carried the Z-car name through the rest of the decade with sharp, wedge-shaped styling that still looks right today. Pop-up headlights, a hybrid digital/analog gauge cluster, and available T-tops made it feel like a spaceship compared with the Datsuns that came before it. Buyers could choose the turbocharged VG30ET or, as here, the naturally aspirated 3.0-liter VG30E in GS trim. That naturally aspirated setup is a big part of this car's charm. It's simple, durable, and rev-happy, and connecting it to a five-speed manual delivers the kind of engaging, analog experience that has made clean '80s Japanese sports cars one of the hottest corners of the collector market. If you've followed the rising interest in these cars, you may remember the 21K-mile 1984 300ZX 50th Anniversary Edition we covered, and survivors with this few miles are only getting harder to find. The first thing that grabs you is the color. Bright Blue Metallic (paint code 426) is a wonderfully period-correct shade, and it's matched inside by blue leather upholstery for a head-to-toe coordinated look that screams late-'80s cool. Removable glass T-top panels let you bring the sky inside, while factory fog lights, alloy wheels (swapped for a set of chrome wheels here), and that long, low profile finish the package. According to the listing, the car stayed with a single owner before the selling dealer acquired it. A State of New Jersey new car dealer inspection sticker is still on the windshield, which is the kind of small detail that makes a survivor like this so charming. The clean CARFAX shows initial New Jersey registration starting in December 1989, followed by later Florida and New Jersey registration. This GS came nicely optioned for its day, with power windows, locks, and mirrors, cruise control, air conditioning, a leather-trimmed steering wheel, bucket seats, and an AM/FM stereo with a power antenna. Power steering and disc brakes round out the list. Ahead of the sale, the selling dealer, Vantage Auto, gave the car a tune-up that included new spark plugs, an oil change, and a brake fluid flush. It comes with its owner's manual, a clean CARFAX report, and a clean New Jersey title. Paint meter readings and detailed condition photos are included in the listing's extensive gallery of more than 300 images, so bidders can see exactly what they're getting. Z31s were built in big numbers, but finding one that hasn't been modified, raced, or used up is another story, and finding one with fewer than 8,000 miles is rarer still. Bidding stood at $3,000 at the time of writing, with the auction scheduled to end Thursday, October 8, at 3:20 p.m. EDT. The car is located in Moonachie, New Jersey. For fans of the later Z32 cars, we've also featured a 34-years-owned 1990 300ZX Twin Turbo on Hagerty Marketplace and a final-year 1996 300ZX five-speed. But if you want the purest expression of the '80s Z-car formula, a blue-on-blue, T-top, five-speed GS with this kind of history is tough to beat. title: How Family Businesses Should Plan for Generational Success - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Companies with significant family ownership generate roughly 70% of global economic output and 60% of the world’s jobs. However, only three in 10 survive to a second generation. In this episode of Goldman Sachs Exchanges, FX de Mallmann, chairman of Goldman Sachs EMEA and chairman of Investment Banking, and Tucker York, chairman of global Wealth Management, discuss why succession is so difficult, how enduring enterprises structure governance, and the mindset shift required after a sale or IPO. Allison Nathan: Welcome to Goldman Sachs Exchanges. I'm Allison Nathan. Here's a number that surprised me when I first read it. Companies where a family still holds a significant stake produce 70% of the world's economic output and 60% of its jobs. But only 3 in 10 reach a second generation. And only about 1 in 10 reaches a third. So, why is that? To help me work through that, I'm joined by two people who see opposite ends of this. FX de Mallmann is Chairman of Goldman Sachs EMEA and Chairman of Investment Banking. He also leads the firm's coverage of large family-owned companies and family offices, which means he's on the corporate side of the table: the capital raises, the IPOs, the sales, and the successions. Tucker York chairs our global wealth management business. He's on the other side: the families, their balance sheets, and the next generation once that capital is created. Allison Nathan: Yes, happy to have you both. So, FX, let's just start with some context here on the size and the scope and the impact of family-owned businesses. I gave a few stats to start us off, but maybe provide a bit more color on that for us. FX de Mallmann: The statistics you quoted are those we included in our recently published report on honoring legacy, which are global statistics. We did dig a little bit deeper into some of the statistics and see how they apply to differ around the world. And what we found is that there is an enormous space on family-owned businesses in all major regions. In the US, for instance, there are over 32 million family-owned businesses, which represent over 80% of all businesses. Those account for over 60% of GDP and over 60% of the overall workforce. If you move from the private company world to the public company world, around 35% of the Fortune 500 companies are family-controlled or have a significant family owner, which is a substantial base. As you move to Europe, there are significant industries that have leaders, companies that are leading the industry, that have either family control or significant family shareholder - in luxury goods, in beauty and cosmetics, in shipping, in consumer goods, in retail, in telco, in business services, in industrial, in defense, in numerous other sectors. The size and scale and the success of some of these entrepreneurs has been outstanding. And as you move to Asia, there are countries where you have very large family conglomerates that control many sectors of the economy that are very diversified, not only vertically, but also horizontally. And you see many of those in India, in Korea, and in numerous other Asia countries where the role that these families play is significant to the economy, but also in their ability to create new businesses and innovate in all the fields where they operate. Allison Nathan: Those numbers are actually absolutely staggering. And I don't think most people think about businesses in that way. If we think about the family-owned businesses, how does the fact of them being family-owned affect how they run and how they operate if you're inside the business? FX de Mallmann: Well, in the word family-owned, there is the word owned. And therefore, each of these businesses tend to be owned or partly owned by an individual or a family that, on average, tend to be both invested economically, financially, but also emotionally in the business and very engaged. And so, we find in our interactions with many of these entrepreneurs that they tend to take a very long-term view on their business. They tend to be rigorous stewards of their management team. They tend to be disciplined allocators of capital. And they also tend to be prudent with respect to the decisions they make, including the investment decisions and their use of leverage. And on balance, a statistic that we have access to show that these businesses, when family controlled, on average, tend to outperform non-family-controlled businesses. Allison Nathan: Tucker, let me bring you into the conversation because you're sitting with these families day-to-day. Again, let me ask you a different version of the question. How does the fact that these businesses are family-owned impact the way they invest? Tucker York: I'll take a step back saying that I agree that the numbers are staggering when you think about the family connectivity to business and GDP, etc. It's worth putting that in context. In the history of civilization, it used to be a much higher percentage than that. It's only in the last couple of centuries where we have more of a corporate structure and the scale that comes from that more permanent capital that comes around that, that's led to this. So, these concepts are age-old, is what I would say. What I find with investors is the moment that you start thinking about next generation, how do you invest? How do you think about those things? As distinct from what do I need to do this week, this month, this quarter? It all turns on a long-term orientation. What do I think is going on in the long-term? How do I think about that? And that juxtaposition between those two things is very different for families who are thinking about next generation and what's going to happen beyond me. Have I created something that will go beyond? And that leads you down to make decisions about where do I think this investment that I make today will be 10 years, 20 years from now? As distinct from where do I think this investment made today will be next quarter when some new information comes out, etcetera, and it goes up or down? Allison Nathan: So, much more longer-term perspective coming from these families and how they manage their businesses. Of course, as you just touched on, Tucker, the big issue they all face is the generational transition, which is a very critical moment, you say FX, both for the businesses and for the families. Talk us through why that is such a critical moment. FX de Mallmann: It's a critical moment because it's a moment where the founder has to make a decision on two topics. Topic number one, should his family, typically his children or any other family members, stay involved in the management, typically the running of the business? And if so, in what capacity? And the second decision is how is he or she going to pass on the stock, the ownership of the company from one generation to the next? And what's the organization he set up in order to do that successfully? The statistics you mentioned before that only a third of the businesses pass on to the second generation, about 10% to the third, in our view, is neither good nor bad. It kind of is what it is. What's important is, does the business benefit from that family ownership? Or does the business benefit from having a broader ownership base? We have seen outstanding case studies in both, some businesses with one founder who decided that it absolutely should not stay within the family, diversify the ownership, brought in professional management and the companies scaled to be enormously successful companies. And we've seen other examples where the founder took absolutely the reverse view. And the business actually tremendously benefited in being controlled and typically also managed by the family. The key question in our view on experience is, what's the process around this decision making? How early in advance is this considered? And what are the mechanisms to make sure the right judgments are exercised, both on the ability of the family to continue to manage and on how to best organize the ownership and make sure the ownership structure and governance survive the passage of time? Allison Nathan: And Tucker, this ultimately all comes down to succession plans. But you found that only about half of the businesses, family businesses, actually have succession plans, but mostly informal. And only about a third actually write down these plans. So, why is it so hard when this is so critical to their future? Tucker York: I think business succession, like all businesses, go through that and the businesses that are well run have a better succession plan. I think with the family-owned, it's super complicated because one thing is what does the founder want? But it's also, well, what does the next generation want? And the fact is that while business is dynamic, and it's impacted by things you can control, but oftentimes things you can't control like the economy, industry, competition, etc. Families are impacted that way too. And families change and grow. Next generation tends to get married to other people, which brings other people into the mix, etc. And so, all of these things make it very complicated. It's certainly a best practice to write some things down. We would agree with that. But what is written down and the flexibility around what is written down to be able to adapt to new circumstances and things that come down the pike is vitally important. And so, having a plan is a really good thing from a structure standpoint. But it's also a really good thing to make sure there is flexibility built in to allow for things that will inevitably occur. FX de Mallmann: I wanted to just pick up on your question, Allison. In my experience, many of these founder owners tend initially, certainly in their lifetime, to be extremely busy, extremely preoccupied and engaged in their business. And often prioritize their business over long-term planning. Often this is for the right reason to the great benefit of the business. And then the second key factor is orchestrating and considering this decision forces some pretty hard judgments, some of which they're able to do at a certain point in time, some of which they'd rather have more time to consider, including is their family, are their children capable? Do they have the relevant experience or desire to be involved in the business? Some cases it's too early to judge. Many of these founders decide that taking more time and having more visibility with the passage of time will de-risk some of these decisions. Allison Nathan: And as you said, FX, it's a process. Because you have these creators, they're focused on growing their business. But at some point, they do transition to thinking about how the business is going to outlive them. So, what does that transition look like, especially for families that do this well? FX de Mallmann: That process really involves facing those two questions. Should my family, any family members be involved in the business itself in a management role, junior or senior, but over time, senior, yes or no? And how do I organize the ownership to be transferred from one generation to the other? On the first one, my own view is it's a very delicate judgment, but really relies on is there someone who is capable, who has the relevant experience, and who has a desire to rise up to the occasion. That judgment needs to be as independent as possible. Typically, the founder is the absolute best person to render that judgment. In some cases, we see them soliciting external input to benchmark or compare their own family members with external talent. And what we find on average is the larger the company, the more global, the more complex, typically, the more likely it will require a non-family member with significant experience to continue to run it. And we see many family businesses choosing to bring professional management as they scale up. On the second, which is a question of how does the ownership get passed on, the initial typical approach is to say, let's divide the ownership equally between the number of children or sort of second-generation family members. The question that brings is, what's the organization of that group? How large is that group? Has any member got the right to exit if she wants to or he wants to? And what's the mechanism to exit? And how do any conflicts get tackled and resolved? Is this within the family or is this with a governance structure that allows the resolution of conflict? And in my experience, this process and this mechanism needs to be thought through early on before the number of family members gets too large. And typically, having some exit right of some form and having some conflict resolution mechanism in case there is one or disagreement on any point goes a long way. Allison Nathan: And as we touched on, it's not necessarily just about the family dynamics. There's a whole world, there's an economic cycle, because ultimately, they can pass on and keep the business in the family. But there's also the ability to IPO. There's the ability to sell outright. So, how big of a driver are these other factors when you're talking to families as they work through this? FX de Mallmann: In many cases, one of the questions the companies face, and the family faces is, does the company need external capital to scale the business? And typically, when there is a capital need, it brings the question of who are the investors, what's the source of capital, and by how much should the family get diluted as part of that? That's one big aspect. A second aspect, and we've seen numerous examples of this, is a number of families decide and believe that bringing a third-party investor, whether it's a single investor or a group of investors, and it could also be the public market, can be a source of discipline and a forcing mechanism around many aspects that may be complicated to discuss or resolved within the family. Some choose to sell either because they believe it's the right thing for their business or the right thing for the family. What I have witnessed many times in the context of the sale is there could be great economic outcomes and great solutions for businesses to be consolidated, merged or sold, but that often the family has part of its identity in the business and a sale has a significant impact on the family's emotions and on their sense of identity that's tied to the business. Tucker York: Allison, just to tack on to that from FX both expertise, but also, if you will, the objective is to take care of the health and well-being of the business. In doing that, he's interacting directly with the founder/CEO. It's a different element about, I'll call it, the health and well-being of the family and what's in their best interest. And sometimes it's aligned and sometimes it's not. I think the other thing, too, for any succession planning or any long-term capital structure planning, that also changes over time. And so, this concept of we're going to make a plan and then we're good, it doesn't apply. It needs to be reviewed and stress-tested regularly. In the same way, as you think about next generation planning, most parents, when they think about their children, it's a different set of circumstances when they're 35 than when they're five, and how to think about that. And so, again, it's a regular review of where we are in the process. FX de Mallmann: Tucker, I think you raise just an excellent point on this, which is typically in the first generation, the interests of the business are very aligned and mirror the interests of the family. If it's one individual, it's his business. That's his life or her life. FX de Mallmann: As a number of generations passes, the family's interests may differ from the business interest, and being very clear on whether that's the case, where do they align and where do they differ, is step number one in long-term planning. Tucker York: On the same line, that founder is the shareholder. And so, what they want to do for the business and what they want to do for their wealth creation is the same. And many founders say, "One of the things I want to do with this is I want to give this business to the next generation." There are other founders who say, "What I want to do is I want to give the advantages that I have to the next generation, but I want them to do something different or whatever they want, or etc." And all of those things, again, as that next generation grows, the complexity around that grows as well. Allison Nathan: So, that gets to the wealth creation aspect of this, Tucker, which you have a lot of insight into. Because ultimately, the day a founder sells the company or takes it public, they end up with wealth. And it basically becomes like this pile of money that they have never had to manage before, versus a business that they were managing day in and day out. How do the largest families navigate this and handle this? Tucker York: Well, it's not necessarily what they started out for, but it is an outcome of the success they have and how they think about that, how they think about the way an endowment would think about its money. What is this money for? What is its purpose? What are the other, not only wealth that I want to pass along, but what are the values I want to pass along? And all of that comes into the thing. And yes, so the mindset does change over time. Allison Nathan: And not just the mindset, the organizational structure, the resources required to manage this wealth that is now outside the business versus in the business changes. Tucker York: For sure. And I think it's varied how that works. Some people say, "Well, I want to set up now a new business whose job it is to manage the wealth that I created." Others would say, "I don't aspire to be in that business. I realize that I have to 'take care of these resources in a different way than when it was all in the business'" and they go in different routes. And the reality is, this is what's very interesting about the roles that we get to play is it runs the range. There isn't everybody does it this way or that way. They think about different things. And again, that's where family comes into play as well. FX de Mallmann: Allison, if I just can add one thing on this, we're also seeing in this process, often important differences between first generation family members who involve the business and who often have limited time or choose to spend limited time on allocating or managing the capital that's outside the business. Versus the second generation and onwards who inherit a lot of wealth and a lot of capital and who's one of the important projects, but also responsibilities, is to be good stewards of this capital. And Tucker and his team have a lot of experience with the dynamic between the first generation, the second generation, and the amount of time and effort and resources that each individual family members or branches choose to or want to spend in managing their own assets. Allison Nathan: We end this conversation how we began it with this long-term mindset that these families have, but to your point, Tucker, with some flexibility so they can adapt to the changing family and business dynamics. But in some ways, my takeaway is in a way, as we talked to our individual investors, people potentially listening to this podcast, there is always an emphasis on long-term planning for your own wealth. That those who plan and think about this succession ultimately end up in a better spot than those who don't. Is that a takeaway here about thinking about always having that long-term plan in your mind? Tucker York: I think it absolutely is. People say long-term oriented, that's a better way to be. But if you take a step back, we live in an incredibly short-term oriented world. And so, it's hard to push against that. The way money is managed, it's nice to be able to see your stock that you own go up and down in price. But if it goes up a lot, you're tempted to sell, then you pay taxes, and you have to figure out what to do with it again. If you're in a private company or a private equity, you're holding it for a longer period of time, but then you don't have the flexibility if you need the money to do this thing. What I would argue is it leans towards people should be thinking about staying consistently invested. And a safer way to do that is to not just own one thing, but to own a portfolio of things. So, that on average, the market goes higher over a period of time if you believe in global GDP growth. But that to me is the takeaway. These extraordinary families that have built the enterprises that FX deals with regularly, they have made concentrated bets in one, basically, company that becomes a stock. And that's a way for tremendous wealth creation. But it's incredibly risky. And the things that we don't talk about on podcasts like that are the many other people who tried that and it didn't work. And so, again, you blend the two together. It's owning equity, but doing it in a diversified way and staying consistently long or invested. Allison Nathan: FX, anything to add in terms of a closing message? FX de Mallmann: I fully agree. And what we've seen is many of these entrepreneurs that have created extraordinary businesses have played the long game. They have deployed capital, they have adjusted and adapted their business and investment decisions through many cycles, including volatile times, but they remain invested. And many of those and many families that have benefited from this, it's not only to remain invested, but to continue to invest, whether it's adding capital, buying back stock in the market in their own businesses through the cycle to increase their ownership. So, these are very concentrated bets. But when you have very disciplined, long-term stewards of capital that know and understand the business and are able to attract and retain great management and make disciplined decisions with respect to their family ownership, you typically have a winning recipe for great success and great value creation. title: The Suzuki Adventure Bike That Rivals The BMW GS At A Lower Price - Top Speed
content: Subscribe to the TopSpeed newsletter to never miss an update The adventure bike segment has never been more competitive, yet one name continues to cast a long shadow over every rival: the BMW GS. BMW essentially invented the adventure bike category with the R 80 G/S in the early 1980s, and the GS lineage has carried that benchmark status ever since. The problem? BMW has never been known for keeping prices reasonable. Even the middleweight F 900 GS carries a starting price that climbs well past $14,000 in base trim — and that's before you start ticking option boxes. The good news is that you don't need a German budget to live out your adventure fantasies. Suzuki's V-Strom 800DE makes a compelling case for itself in the middleweight ADV class: a Dakar-inspired machine that pairs Japanese reliability with genuine off-road capability, all at a price that significantly undercuts the BMW. It strikes a near-perfect balance of everyday usability, long-haul comfort, and go-anywhere confidence — without the premium price tag. Here's why the V-Strom 800DE deserves a serious look. Within Suzuki's V-Strom lineup, the V-Strom 800DE is the most off-road-focused model in the family — equally at home on the daily commute and a cross-continental journey. It is powered by a tractable parallel-twin engine, complemented by fully adjustable Showa suspension and long-distance ergonomics. Wrapped in a Dakar-inspired design, the V-Strom can be yours for well under $12,000. That bang-for-buck appeal is only reinforced by Suzuki's well-earned reputation for low running costs and long-term reliability. The BMW F 900 GS, by comparison, starts at over $14,000. That's not to say the V-Strom is perfect, though. The value-focused formula does come with trade-offs. It doesn't produce nearly as much power or torque as the BMW F 900 GS, nor is it among the lightest bikes in the class. It also misses out on some notable features, including cruise control, tubeless tires, and radial-mount brake calipers — which is partly why it's often overlooked in the segment. Look past those shortcomings, however, and you'll find a terrific adventure bike that covers everything you'd actually need your ADV to do, without breaking the bank. Unlike the V-Strom 650 and 1050, the V-Strom 800 uses a parallel-twin engine shared with the GSX-8R and GSX-8S — a pairing that speaks to the motor's versatile character. According to Suzuki, the engine is tuned for smooth, controllable low-end torque while still revving freely to its peak power output. It produces just over 80 horsepower, which is more than sufficient for everyday riding, off-road excursions, and long-distance touring, even if it falls short of the F 900 GS on paper. The absence of a V-twin may give some traditional V-Strom fans pause, but in practice you're not missing much. The engine retains a V-twin-like character courtesy of its 270-degree firing order. It's also notable as the first Suzuki production motorcycle to feature a cross balancer, which enables a more compact, lightweight layout. The result is a powerplant that occupies less space than a V-twin while delivering similar power pulses that enhance traction and strong low-rpm tractability. Parallel-twin, 270-degree crankshaft, DOHC, liquid-cooled Suzuki says the engine is also tuned for good fuel economy, and according to its UK website, it returns just over 53 US MPG in combined conditions. That's respectable efficiency for a do-it-all ADV, and with the 5.3-gallon fuel tank, you can expect a range of over 280 miles between fuel stops. The Suzuki Clutch Assist System (SCAS) and a bidirectional quickshifter round out the package, making gear changes smoother whether you're filtering through city traffic or cruising the highway. The V-Strom 800DE is the most off-road-capable V-Strom currently on sale, and that's where it closes the gap with the F 900 GS most convincingly. It's built around a steel backbone frame tuned for straight-line stability and nimble handling. According to Suzuki, the chassis keeps the bike composed on the highway while remaining easy to thread through trails and forest roads. The one notable downside is a curb weight of over 500 pounds — on the heavier side for the segment. The frame is paired with Showa suspension designed to deliver comfort and performance across all surfaces. Full adjustability gives riders the freedom to dial in behavior to suit their style and load. With 8.7 inches of travel at both ends and the highest ground clearance in the V-Strom family, the 800DE inspires the confidence to tackle obstacles without scraping the engine cases. Showa Linkage-type monoshock, fully adjustable, 8.7 in. travel Dual 310mm discs with Nissin two-piston floating calipers A 21-inch front spoke wheel makes the V-Strom 800DE even more off-road capable, providing better stability on trails and a smoother ride on broken pavement. The 17-inch rear spoke wheel handles grip and comfort at the back. Both wheels are shod in Dunlop Trailmax Mixtour tires with a semi-block pattern that balances off- and on-road traction. Braking duties are handled by a pair of Nissin axial-mount calipers up front and a single unit at the rear. One look at the V-Strom 800DE and its new-generation Suzuki identity is unmistakable — the aggressive, mass-forward design is sharp and contemporary, and it looks particularly striking in the Champion Yellow No. 2 colorway. The Glass Sparkle Black option is equally appealing for those who prefer a more understated look. Either way, Suzuki says the modern styling draws inspiration from the legendary DR-Z Dakar racer and the DR-Big dual sport, with a focus on long-distance comfort and off-road ease. The wide, tapered handlebar is cast in strong yet flexible aluminum, allowing it to absorb shock during off-road riding. The wider grips are designed to remain comfortable in a variety of conditions, including when standing on the pegs. Speaking of which, the footpegs are broad and fitted with vibration-dampening rubber inserts that can be removed for extra grip on the trails. Suzuki says the seat is both supportive and narrow, keeping it comfortable over long distances while remaining accessible for a wide range of rider heights. The front cowl and windscreen are wind-tunnel tested to reduce buffeting on the rider while maximizing visibility from the saddle. The windshield is adjustable across three positions, though you'll need a hex tool to undo and redo the four screws each time. That's a genuine miss on Suzuki's part — most rivals offer tool-free windscreen adjustment. On the plus side, the clutch and brake levers can be adjusted without any tools at all. The V-Strom 800DE's electronics suite is where the bike's budget-conscious nature is most apparent. The package centers on a 5-inch TFT display — smaller than what the F 900 GS offers — and the Suzuki Intelligent Ride System (S.I.R.S.), which bundles traction control, rider modes, a quickshifter, easy start, and low RPM assist. Notably absent are a six-axis IMU and cruise control, even as optional extras. Suzuki partially compensates with a solid range of Genuine Suzuki Accessories, including side and top cases, an engine guard, center stand, low and high seat options, heated grips, and auxiliary lamps. There's also the V-Strom 800DE Adventure variant, which adds a durable aluminum bash plate and aluminum panniers as standard equipment. For context, the BMW F 900 GS offers a more extensive optional extras catalog, including Keyless Ride, TPMS, Sport suspension, a high windscreen, the BMW Motorrad ConnectedRide Navigator, and more. It's clear that the V-Strom 800DE is a more straightforward package than the BMW GS — but holding that against it misses the point entirely. The V-Strom isn't trying to dazzle you with outright performance or a long features list. Instead, it's built to nail the fundamentals of a middleweight adventure bike: friendly power delivery, long-distance comfort, genuine off-road ability, and essential rider aids. It's a solid ADV that gives you everything you actually need, without charging you for the bells and whistles you may never use. We want to hear from you. While he didn’t struggle, he ended the season without a flourish or without hitting some favorable benchmarks (ERA under 3.00, 200+ strikeouts), and as such, I think that ship has sailed. Regardless, McLean’s 2026 was a total success in just about every measure, with the right-hander being well above-average all year except for a stretch in May. McLean might not be the best pitcher in baseball, but the Mets certainly have their ace. Who would’ve foreseen this back in April, when he was struggling? His 118 wRC+ and 4.1 fWAR/4.2 rWAR are the most by a Mets rookie since Pete Alonso’s 2019 Rookie of the Year season. Whether or not this level of play is his high-water mark or something that can be counted on remains to be seen, but there are no ifs, ands, or buts about it, Benge should have a spot on the Mets roster for years to come. Then, he had a brief cup of coffee at the end of the season, and things have been all awry since then. It was reported that the Mets altered his arm slot, lowering it to ensure that, in the words of Eric Jaegers, it did not “tak[e] away from some other things”- meaning his secondary pitches- and sought to “diversify [his] arsenal” by adding a new cutter grip to his repertoire. I don’t remember where I read the tagline, but on the matter, somebody wrote something along the lines of “Jonah Tong is being reshaped to fit the Mets’ vision” rather than developed as what he already is. His fastball lost a few crucial inches of induced vertical break and became less effective. His new cutter was brutalized by Triple-A hitters. His command took a step back as compared to prior years. None of this is to say that Jonah Tong was perfect prior to the 2026 season, but the right-hander struggled for most of the year, and a lot of that seems to have been self-inflicted by the organization. He looked better towards the end of the season and ended things on a high note in his last game of the season against Washington, so here’s hoping that Tong learns from everything he went through this season and comes back in 2027 a better pitcher. Two days later, on May 12, he drove in a run with an RBI triple off of Enmanual De Jesus, having already drawn three walks, in a Mets 10-2 blowout of the Detroit Tigers. It feels crazy now, but five months ago, AJ Ewing was still in Double-A. The 21-year-old has not been as consistent as his fellow rookie outfielder Carson Benge and is still much more a work-in-progress, but there’s a very good chance the team has found its long-term centerfielder. He struggled early in the season and then missed most of June and all of July due to separate groin and hip injuries. He returned to the field in August healthy and posted numbers that are more like Jacob Reimer, but he fell apart once again at the end of the season. Since being drafted in 2022, the infielder’s career has felt like a see-saw: one year he’ll be good, then he’ll have a down year due to injuries, then he’ll recover and be good, then he’ll have a down year due to injuries. Despite 512 at-bats under his belt at the Double-A level split between 2025 and 2026 and a cumulative .252/.352/.424 batting line to show for it, I would assume that the 22-year-old is a lock to be added to the 40-man roster to protect him from the 2026 Rule 5 Draft (if that even takes place). Here’s hoping that 2027 will be an upswing year for him. From June 1 on, he hit a staggering .113/.223/.186 in 49 games- a wRC+ of 10- leading to him being placed on the Developmental List from mid-August until September. He recovered a bit in September, but there are no two ways around it: this was a disastrous season for Clifford. Complicating matters further, there were some fairly high expectations of him in more than a few circles- with Pete Alonso not being re-signed and Clifford knocking on the door, the possibility was there that the slugger could play his way into a role at some point in 2026. Those two independent storylines merged in quite possibly one of, if not the, biggest Mets minor league disappointments of the 2026 season. He missed almost four months due to an oblique injury, and in the games that he pitched prior to being placed on the injured list and after being activated from it, he wasn’t good either. Because of the injury, it’s hard to evaluate whether or not the right-hander was overmatched against Double-A hitters, or if he was pitching compromised because of it. Either way, 2026 was a lost year for him and he is hopefully fully healthy and ready to go in April 2026. April: 5 G (5 GS), 22.1 IP, 16 H, 5 R, 4 ER (1.61 ERA), 12 BB, 26 K, .273 BABIP (Triple-A) May: 5 G (4 GS), 22.2 IP, 19 H, 13 R, 10 ER (3.97 ERA), 13 BB, 20 K, .262 BABIP (Triple-A) June: 5 G (3 GS), 23.0 IP, 23 H, 17 R, 15 ER (5.87 ERA), 14 BB, 22 K, .262 BABIP (Triple-A) July: 4 G (4 GS), 18.1 IP, 18 H, 11 R, 10 ER (4.91 ERA), 11 BB, 16 K, .333 (Triple-A) August: 4 G (3 GS), 18.0 IP, 8 H, 11 R, 10 ER (5.00), 11 BB, 26 K, .129 BABIP (Triple-A) September: 3 G (3 GS), 10.2 IP, 16 H, 9 R, 9 ER (7.59 ERA), 7 BB, 13 K, .455 BABIP (Triple-A) 2026 Season: 26 G (22 GS), 115.0 IP, 100 H, 66 R, 58 ER (4.54 ERA), 68 BB, 123 K, .281 BABIP (Triple-A) Jack Wenninger’s season began strong, but a few months into the 2026 season, the train derailed and he just was not able to get things back on track. His fastball doesn’t really have the best shape and is more of a set-up pitch than a strikeout pitch, but it certainly did its job and effectively set-up his changeup, which was a true plus pitch in 2026, limiting batters to a .175/.245/.299 batting line with a 47.6% Whiff Rate. Outside of that fastball-changeup combination though, Wenninger really had nothing. Batters hit .293/.378/.509 against his sliders; his sweeping slider (.152/.263/.273) was quite a bit better than his gyro slider (.349/.423/.602), but was used a fraction of the amount (23.3% to 8.9%). Further complicating everything was that the right-hander, who came into the season known as a pitcher with good command and control, had trouble against the more experienced Triple-A hitters who also had the ABS system on their side, and his walk rate suffered. There’s still potential in Wenninger, but the right-hander still feels like he is a change or two away from being a potential major league contributor. When he was promoted to Binghamton, almost overnight, Voit became one of, if not the, most exciting players in the minor league system. In 29 games with the Rumble Ponies, he posted a wRC+ of 158- and that takes into account a little lull that he had in September; remove those 7 games, and he had a 202 wRC+ against Eastern League pitchers. Early on in the season, Voit began working with his hitting coaches to refine his decisions at the plate and to focus on swinging at good pitches and making good contact, putting extra effort into studying scouting reports and figuring out how to get pitchers to work to his strengths rather than him falling into their pitching traps. By the time the summer began, he was doing just that, and the results spoke for themselves. Some of the underlying metrics propping up his numbers are unsustainable- no player in major league history since LD% began being tracked has ever posted a 30% LD% and a BABIP over .400- so expect some likely regression in 2027, but if the infielder can continue producing even a fraction of the number he produced during the dog days of the summer, that’s money. When the southpaw was promoted to Triple-A Syracuse, things went poorly at first, but by the time the end of the season rolled around, he righted the ship to a degree; In his first four Triple-A starts, he allowed 12 earned runs in 14.0 innings, allowing 16 hits, walking 16, and striking out 18 and in his final four Triple-A starts, he allowed 8 earned runs in 20.1 innings, allowing 18 hits, walking 5, and striking out 25. The left-hander corrected his atrocious walk rate, but in throwing more pitches in the zone, let himself get hurt by the long ball; his home run rate spiked, allowing 5 home runs in those 20.1 innings, as opposed to 1 over the course of his first four starts, and 4 over the course of all 90.2 innings he pitched in Binghamton. I think that encapsulates Santucci as a pitcher- he is most effective when pitching around the zone and getting batters to get themselves out rather than dominating them in it, so it will be interesting to see how he fares in a larger Triple-A sample size next season. By most metrics, he was pitching above his head and is likely to regress, but the Mets don’t need Thornton to be 20% better than the average National League pitcher for their rotation to be in a good place going forward- it certainly wouldn’t hurt, though. In 114 games with the Syracuse Mets, who play in the International League where offense was plentiful this past year, he only hit .254/.355/.388 (96 wRC+) with poor underlying batted ball data and metrics. At the same time, he made the MLB roster, and despite his overall struggles in limited action with the Mets, he achieved what 99% of other kids who put on their gloves and dream of being big leaguers don’t. With his speed Morabito is a useful player to have around, but with his offensive limitations, it is hard to really expect much if anything from him. On the eve of its 10-year anniversary, Rancho Santa Fe restaurant Nick & G’s will be undergoing a complete renovation and menu refresh. The eatery will close in mid-October and reopen with a brand new look in November. The update will include a redesigned indoor dining room and bar, and new private event and patio spaces. A California-Italian-inspired menu will feature handmade pastas, pizzas and seasonal shared plates. The Lilian Rice building at the corner of Paseo Delicias and La Granada has a long history, originally built in the 1920s and serving as the home of the Millar family, one of the earliest Rancho Santa Fe families. It was previously Delicias restaurant for 24 years and briefly Ponsaty’s. Local resident Sandra DiCicco-Bonar of the Grand Restaurant Group took over and opened Nick & G’s in 2017, naming it after her children Nicolas and Gianina. “As we approach our 10th anniversary, we wanted to honor what our guests have always loved about Nick & G’s while creating something fresh for the next chapter, said Gianina Pickens, the “G” of Nick and G’s, and chief operating officer of Grand Restaurant Group. ”It’s incredibly meaningful to continue our family’s hospitality legacy in a place that has become such a special part of the Rancho Santa Fe community.” Leading the restaurant group, Pickens is carrying on her family’s culinary heritage that goes back to her grandfather Nicola DiCicco, who emigrated from Pacentro, Italy, and built a family restaurant business with his four brothers starting in the Fresno area, according to a news release. Chef/Partner Alex Carballo has joined Pickens in the renovation effort. Carballo has been with the Grand Restaurant Group for about a year, bringing a resume that spans 20 years in the local San Diego hospitality scene, including stops at Stone Brewing World Bistro & Gardens and Fox Point Farms—he was also the chef at The Crosby Club when it first opened. In addition to Nick & G’s, Carballo is also overseeing the Grand Restaurant Group’s newly reimagined Nómada in Carlsbad and recently announced Bangers BBQ, set to open next year in Escondido. In Rancho Santa Fe Carballo is working to bring his vision to life, with his hands on everything from tinkering with the menu to picking plants for the patio. He understands his mission to deliver  a high-quality dining experience, “meeting the high expectations that this community does have.” Carballo’s design inspiration was developed in consultation with Rachael Lorraine Harris and Michael Soriano. The look will invoke the energy of the Amalfi Coast, brighter, lighter and more contemporary, bringing in very different shades of yellow, orange and blue with lots of greenery and nature-inspired patterns. A grandiose olive tree will take root at the center of the dining room, which will feature all-new custom-made banquettes and tables. Guests will be able to see through to the updated, lightened-up bar and lounge through a beautiful new wine cellar. They will also be able to see into the kitchen. “You should feel like you’re taken away someplace else,” Carballo said of his vision. “In Rancho Santa Fe you already get that amongst the trees and beautiful Spanish architecture… to enter the restaurant you will see and feel the difference, feel the warmth and nature.” They hope to create a “wow” vibe inside, but they also hope the outdoor spaces will be places people will want to spend some time. The patio will be lush with plants with a new wave shade canopy overhead, and the courtyard in the back will have a garden feel with more greenery and water features. Carballo is still crafting the new menu—some Nick & G’s favorites will remain, but the update will focus on coastal Italian-Americana dishes, a smaller and fine-tuned menu showcasing the best local produce, handmade pasta and seafood. He will spend the downtime during construction working on wine pairing, hiring new people, training on service and learning the menu. Having started out years ago in Rancho Santa Fe, Carballo is part of a close-knit family of local chefs that includes people such as Johnny Freyberg at The Crosby and Patrick Ponsaty at The Inn. Nick & G’s has continued to build relationships and collaborate with the Rancho Santa Fe community—they recently teamed up to host an exclusive multi-course Patrimony Estate wine dinner. Nick & G’s hopes to continue offering experiences like that with live music, special dinners and community events. Carballo is excited by the village revitalization that now includes several different dining options such as Paseo and the newly opened Paseo Pizza & Gelato, the new Rancho Sandwich and Creamery, the mainstay of Mille Fleurs, Lilian’s and the cafe at The Inn and spots like Thyme in the Ranch, Caffe Positano and Rancho Roasters. And coming soon, a new Nick & G’s. “I like the energy when there’s more…it gives people a little more variety and a reason to go into Rancho Santa Fe, and we’re in the heart of it,” Carballo said. “I’m glad that the family and partners are trusting me to take this and show the community we’re here to stay and give them something new and great to look forward to.” For updates ahead of the reopening, follow along at nickandgs.com and @nickandgs on Instagram. title: Wide Open GS Title Battle Entering Road Atlanta Finale - Sportscar365
content: Forty-five cars set for Friday’s season-ending Fox Factory 120 at Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta… Under the current IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge points structure introduced in 2021, there’s been an 80 percent hit rate of drivers leading the points at the second-to-last race and securing the championship at the Michelin Raceway Road Atlanta season finale. The two times out of ten it didn’t happen, the lead was 30 points or less. First-time 2026 GS championship leaders Austin Krainz and Stevan McAleer in the No. 27 AutoTechnic Racing BMW M4 GT4 EVO come to the Fox Factory 120 with a lead of exactly 30 points. Krainz and McAleer haven’t won but have been the model of consistency for two years straight. They can only clinch outright with a win; otherwise, they’ll need to finish ahead of their rivals. This year, they’ve finished between second and 11th in eight of nine races, and only have a worst result of 17th. They’re the fifth different GS entry to lead the championship this year, following the No. 71 Rebel Rock Racing Aston Martin Vantage GT4 Evo, No. 57 Winward Racing Mercedes-AMG GT GT4, No. 95 Turner Motorsport BMW M4 GT4 EVO and No. 13 McCumbee McAleer Racing Ford Mustang GT4. Emblematic of the topsy-turvy nature of 2026, Krainz and McAleer’s pre-Michelin Raceway point total of 2,190 points is the lowest entering the final round by any GS leader since the current points system was introduced. They’re ahead of the aforementioned No. 95 Turner BMW featuring past GS champions Dillon Machavern (2017) and Luca Mars (2025) by 30 points and Robert Noaker in the No. 13 MMR Ford by 40. Both Turner and MMR have second entries this race, including MMR’s debuting No. 61 Ford Mustang GT4 of Jenson Altzman and Erik Evans. Fourth-placed Michael Cooper and Moisey Uretsky (120 back, No. 44 Ibiza Farm Motorsport McLaren Artura GT4) and fifth-placed Bryce Ward (130 back, No. 57 Winward Mercedes-AMG) are in with a mathematical shot. Cooper and Uretsky won both at Indianapolis last race and Michelin Raceway last year. Wild point swings can occur with up to a maximum 340-point swing between first (350 points) and 30th (10). The only GS second-place entry to leap to first at the finale in the last five years occurred in 2021. Jan Heylen and Ryan Hardwick won the finale aboard Wright Motorsports’ No. 16 Porsche 718 Cayman GT4 Clubsport RS, which propelled Heylen from 30 points down entering the finale to the championship by 190 points over Turner Motorsport’s Machavern and Bill Auberlen and Machavern, who had a fraught finale en route to 18th in their No. 95 BMW M4 GT4. Subsequent leaders have held leads of 160, 60, 110 and 100 points in GS the last four years and have brought it home. TCR should have no such challenges this year. Mason Filippi and Bryson Morris entered Indianapolis with a 260-point lead in their No. 33 Bryan Herta Autosport Hyundai Elantra N TCR and left it with a 200-point margin over teammates Denis Dupont and Preston Brown in the similar No. 76 Herta Hyundai. That puts them well in line with past champions who entered the finale with 230, 100, 20 and 100-point gaps and then brought it home. Only last year did TCR see a last-race points change. MMG’s No. 93 Honda Civic FL5 TCR of LP Montour and Karl Wittmer had a race fraught with mechanical maladies, opening the door for Harry Gottsacker to overcome a 10-point – or one position – points deficit and claim his second TCR title (2023). Provided Filippi and Morris start the season finale, they’ll score at least last-place points and have enough in hand to wrap the title, which would extend Herta and Hyundai’s run of title form where both team and manufacturer have won six TCR titles in the last seven years. Hyundai has won the last six manufacturer titles (2020 through 2025) and all driver titles since 2019, except 2024. It’d be a first for both drivers, though. As for the race itself, four different TCR brands have won at Road Atlanta in the last five years. All of Alfa Romeo, Honda, Hyundai and Cupra have won since 2021. There are 45 cars entered for the finale, split 31 GS and 14 TCR. Pilot Challenge teams practice Wednesday, September 30 and Thursday, October 1 with qualifying Thursday evening at 6:25 p.m. ET. The FOX Factory 120 streams live on Friday, October 2, at 11:35 a.m. ET on Peacock and live, flag-to-flag, ad-free courtesy of Michelin on the IMSA Official YouTube channel. title: Grand Seiko SBGH376 "Sakura Wakaba" | HANDS ON - Time+Tide Watches
content: Did you catch the Grand Seiko SBGH376 “Sakura Wakaba” when it came out? At Watches and Wonders 2026, much of the focus was on the Grand Seiko Ushio Diver – and understandably so. But this precious SBGH376 was another more under-the-radar Grand Seiko launch that was not one to miss. The diver is a daily, but for many, this SBGH376 could be a grail. The Grand Seiko SBGH376 “Sakura Wakaba” comes in what may be my personal favourite Grand Seiko case geometry: the 62GS. The 62GS shape stands out with its highly faceted design, somehow both sharp and rounded at the same time. In my opinion, it is one of the best geometries in the brand’s arsenal to show off its renowned, top-notch Zaratsu finishing. And in 18k yellow gold, the Zaratsu finishing looks even more potent. Studio Shizukuishi, the home of Grand Seiko’s fully mechanical watchmaking, and Studio Shinshu, the brand’s home for its quartz and Spring Drive creations, often have subtle deviations in finishing style for the various case geometries. In the case of the 62GS, pun not intended, Studio Shizukuishi renders the 62GS steel case with a full distortion-free mirror polish on the front of the case and the upper half of the case sides. But were you to look at Grand Seiko’s titanium SBGA413 ‘Shunbun’, a fan-favourite creation out of Studio Shinshu, the front of the lugs would be hairline brushed. For white metal cases in steel or titanium, I personally prefer the brushed-leading Shinshu way. But in the case of 18k yellow gold, ok that time pun intended, I think the design benefits from leading with distortion-free mirror finishing. It results in the case going dark when viewed head-on under light, letting the vibrant dial be the focal point as you’re trying to read the time. But, of course, you still have some rich hairline brushing on the case sides – and the lines that are much richer in the yellow gold hue. In terms of fit, the SBGH376 is in Grand Seiko’s 38mm 62GS case, which also measures 12.9mm thick and a nice compact 44.7mm lug-to-lug to better suit a more dress-watch-oriented scale. But, to be clear, this watch is 100 metres water-resistant with a screw-down crown – so it’s not the case in this instance that would give you pause for taking it for a swim. If the 18k yellow gold case wasn’t already eye-catching enough, the co-star in the SBGH376 equation is its Sakura Wakaba dial that captures the moment when white cherry blossoms and fresh green leaves appear together – the transition from sakura blossoms to budding leaves in Japan’s springtime. In plainer terms, the dial is a light green dial with a foliage-inspired texture created through a sort of crosshatched texture pressed into the dial with a handcrafted mould. The razor-sharp hands, faceted hour indices, date window frame, and GS logo are executed in a case-matching tone – but they are not solid gold, as there is no special star signature on the dial, which Grand Seiko utilises to denote when precious metal is used for dial components. Nonetheless, the finishing of these components is superb, and I always love Grand Seiko’s razor-sharp dauphine-style handset when they are mirror-polished on their top side. You can watch the gold-toned central seconds hand pass over the hands and see the distortion-free reflection that reveals just how well these hands are finished. Now, the strap is where you cannot really take full advantage of the 100-metre depth rating. The SBGH376 is handsomely outfitted on a brown crocodile leather strap with an 18k yellow gold folding clasp to secure it to your wrist. It is a perfect pairing as a leather option in my eyes; however, I still want to see Grand Seiko invest in rubber strap making – rubber straps that sit flush to the respective case geometry they are made for as a means to offer a more casual aesthetic that can better cater to the daily-driver specs watches like this have while still being able to be dressed up. Inside and exhibited is Grand Seiko’s in-house high-beat automatic 9S85 movement with 55 hours of power reserve. It’s a great tried-and-true calibre for the brand, regulated to be accurate to +5/-3 seconds per day when static. That said, I’d like to see Grand Seiko start using next-gen calibres like the 9SA5, or an equivalent, in watches like this to make the offer feel even more premium than it already is. At US$32,800 or A$46,600, this is a very aspirational Grand Seiko watch for buyers around the world. Fortunately, it is not a limited edition, so you have time to save up if you don’t have the purse right now. In terms of its aesthetic and dimensions, there is nothing I would really pick apart or change. It’s very well executed and yet another very attractive Grand Seiko design. My two points of feedback as a Grand Seiko fanboy are the calibre being the more entry-level high-beat 9S85 instead of the more advanced 9SA5, which, in fairness, has yet to be in a case smaller than 40mm. But its hand-wound sibling, the 9SA4, has been used in 38mm cases, so having a dual impulse escapement movement from Grand Seiko in a watch this size is not beyond the realm of possibility. The second is the strap. Again, the brown crocodile is classic and suits the watch well, but I do think the right rubber strap with a textile-like upper on a watch like this could work really well and open this reference up to an even broader demographic. title: BMW F 450 GS Review: A Proper Little GS - Bike Rider Magazine
content: BMW’s new F 450 GS brings big-bike technology, a punchy parallel twin and genuine gravel ability to the lightweight adventure class. We test it on road and dirt – with and without BMW’s clever Easy Ride Clutch. BMW’s new F 450 GS might be the smallest member of the GS family, but after riding it on road and gravel, there’s much more big-bike GS DNA here than you might expect. There’s something immediately likeable about the new BMW F 450 GS. In fact, before you even turn a wheel, BMW has got one important thing right – it looks like a proper GS. The distinctive X-shaped headlight borrowed from the bigger members of the family, little beak, familiar GS profile and, particularly in the GS Trophy colours, give the 450 considerably more presence than you might expect from a small-capacity adventure bike. It’s one of those bikes that makes you stop and have a second look. But the more important discovery from our time with the F 450 GS is that the family resemblance goes considerably deeper than the styling. Climb aboard and there’s a surprising amount of big-GS familiarity. The switchgear, BMW’s rotary controller and TFT dash will all be immediately recognisable to anyone who has spent time on BMW’s larger adventure bikes. That makes the F 450 GS feel surprisingly premium for what is now the entry point to the GS family. There are areas where the budget becomes a little more obvious – some of the finishing around the top yoke and ignition, for example – but the stuff you actually interact with is impressively polished. “Before you even turn a wheel, BMW has got one important thing right – it looks like a proper GS.” The riding position is typically upright and comfortable, while an 845mm seat height doesn’t feel intimidating thanks partly to how slim the bike is through the middle. BMW quotes a road-ready, fully fuelled weight of just an impressive 178kg, and you notice it immediately. It’s light, manoeuvrable and unintimidating, whether you’re threading through traffic or picking your way along a gravel road. Our test took place on an exceptionally windy day making it difficult to properly judge the screen, but while there was still plenty happening around the helmet, it did a decent job of keeping the blast away from the torso. The standard two-piece seat is reasonably firm and limits movement forward and back slightly, but if you’re going to get serious on the BMW, then they also offer a taller one-piece Rallye seat as an accessory. And while it will undoubtedly aid movement, I imagine it’ll probably look cooler as well. Despite the name, the new engine actually displaces 420cc. The parallel twin produces 48hp at 8750rpm and 43Nm at 6750rpm, with an unusual 135-degree crankpin offset. And it’s one of the highlights of the bike. The twin is surprisingly smooth, yet still has plenty of character despite delivering its power in a wonderfully linear fashion. There’s useful drive through the middle of the rev range, which makes it easy to manage on loose surfaces, but let it spin beyond 7000rpm and there’s enough enthusiasm at the top to make the F 450 GS surprisingly entertaining on the road. “It’s smooth, has plenty of character and delivers its power in a wonderfully linear fashion.” It doesn’t suddenly come alive with a big top-end hit. Instead, it simply keeps pulling, making it an exceptionally easy engine to use. And despite being the baby GS, I wouldn’t hesitate to take one of these on a decent trip, especially as with a 14-litre tank and BMW claiming consumption of 3.8L/100km, there’s theoretically well over 300km of range available too. We had two F 450 GS examples to play with, which gave us the opportunity to experience rather different versions of the same motorcycle. There was a GS Trophy which featured BMW’s new Easy Ride Clutch, while the Racing Red bike retained the conventional clutch but had been fitted with cross-spoked wheels and much more dirt-focused Metzeler Karoo 4 rubber. And it was the difference in those tyres that was immediately noticeable. On tarmac, the Karoo 4s made the bike feel distinctly different – initially enough that I wondered whether something was wrong with the tyre pressures – but head onto loose surfaces and the extra grip was obvious. The more road-orientated tyres on the Trophy were surprisingly capable on dry gravel but quickly reached their limits once things became wet or muddy. The 19-inch front wheel might not appeal to riders looking for a miniature rally bike, but for the kind of mixed road and gravel riding most Kiwi adventure riders actually do, it works well enough. And, so, onto the big talking point of the new GS, BMW’s Easy Ride Clutch (ERC). There is a multitude of different versions of ‘auto clutch’ available from manufacturers nowadays, with them all seemingly doing it a bit different. And riders also seem to fit into two camps – love them or hate them. I’ve ridden with most of them, and I reckon that the BMW system is probably one of the best, especially for adventure riding. You see, rather than removing the clutch lever altogether, BMW uses a centrifugal clutch that automatically engages according to engine speed. Select first gear at a standstill, release the clutch lever and nothing happens until you open the throttle. Twist the throttle and pick the revs up to 2,500rpm and the drive engages and you start to move forward. It’s pretty easy, and combined with Shift Assistant Pro, you can essentially ride without touching the clutch lever at all. Pull away on the throttle, shift up and down using the quickshifter and come to a complete stop without disengaging the clutch. Yet, BMW has deliberately retained the conventional clutch lever, so the rider can override the system whenever required. “For an adventure bike, that combination makes a lot of sense.” Around town, it works brilliantly. There’s no possibility of stalling when you’re pulling away from the lights and, once you’ve recalibrated your brain, low-speed manoeuvring becomes surprisingly natural. This is a system that will aid with confidence for new riders or those who really struggle with clutch control. Off-road, there is a compromise. Starting from stationary on a slippery surface requires enough throttle for the centrifugal clutch to engage, which can make it easier to spin the rear tyre than when you’re delicately feeding in a conventional clutch. But unlike some automated systems, the lever is still there when you need it. Want to pop the front over an obstacle or deliberately introduce a burst of power? Pull the clutch in, build the revs and release it exactly as you normally would. For an adventure bike, that combination makes a lot of sense. And BMW’s Shift Assistant Pro is excellent. Changes in either direction are slick enough that there really is very little reason to touch the clutch during normal riding. Standing on the pegs reveals another strength of the F 450 GS. It’s beautifully slim through the middle, giving you plenty of room to move around and making it easy to grip the bike with your knees. At six feet tall, I found the handlebar fractionally low when standing, although rotating it slightly forward would probably have improved matters. Otherwise, the ergonomics work well. The suspension is where you begin to find the limits. There’s 180mm of travel at both ends, with a 43mm USD fork and an adjustable rear shock. For gravel roads and relatively gentle off-road riding it’s perfectly adequate, but start hitting bigger holes and sharp bumps with enthusiasm and you can feel the suspension beginning to struggle. “It doesn’t feel like BMW has simply built a cheap 450 and stuck a GS badge on it.” And that’s probably the key to understanding the F 450 GS. This isn’t a lightweight rally bike or an enduro machine wearing indicators. Think of it instead as perhaps 70/30 road to dirt – a smaller, lighter interpretation of what BMW’s larger GS models have always done. You could load it up, ride it down the South Island, spend days exploring gravel roads and ride it home again. That’s much more its natural territory than tackling a technical trail ride. The BMW F 450 GS enters a part of the adventure market that’s becoming increasingly competitive, and its $13,490 + ORC starting price puts it at the premium end of the small-capacity category. Start adding some of the desirable options and that gap can grow further. But there’s also an argument that you’re getting something for that premium. The TFT, electronics, switchgear and overall integration have the polish we’ve become accustomed to on considerably more expensive BMWs. The engine is excellent, the bike is light and extremely easy to manage, and it manages the difficult trick of being friendly to a relatively inexperienced rider without becoming boring for somebody with considerably more experience. Most importantly, it doesn’t feel like BMW has simply got someone to build a cheap 450 and stuck a GS badge on it. And that might turn out to be the F 450 GS’s biggest strength. title: Drake Surprises Karol G’s Houston Crowd With ‘Ahí,’ ‘Janice STFU’ & ‘One Dance’ Performances - Billboard
content:
The rapper joined the Colombian superstar on stage for three surprise tracks. Drake made a surprise appearance at Karol G‘s concert in Houston on Sunday (Sept. 27), joining the Colombian superstar on stage for three performances. In fan-shot clips from the show, both artists appeared dressed in black, with Drake taking the mic at the ending of Karol performing their collaboration “Ahí,” and reciting his line from the track, “I want a Latina, I want a Latina/ I want a G like Karolina.” He then performed his single “Janice STFU” and his 2016 hit “One Dance” as Karol G danced beside him before the two moved in close, drawing roars from the crowd. The appearance was the latest in a series of moments between the two stars. Drake attended Karol G’s Toronto show in July, appearing on the venue’s Jumbotron, and had publicly nodded to her on record before their team-up, name-checking her on “New Bestie” from his 2026 project MAID OF HONOUR. The pair then released “Ahí” in August, and the single made an immediate mark on Billboard‘s Latin charts. It debuted at No. 1 on Hot Latin Songs — Drake’s fourth leader on the tally — and gave him his first career No. 1 on Hot Latin Rhythm Songs, a chart he had never previously topped. Released in 2016, “One Dance” was a career milestone for Drake. Featuring Nigerian star Wizkid and British singer Kyla, it became his first Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 as a lead artist, spent 10 weeks atop the chart and reigned for years as the most streamed song in Spotify history. It has since become a staple of his unannounced guest spots, including a surprise set at Vybz Kartel’s Toronto concert last year, where he also performed it. For Karol G, the moment adds to a genre-reshaping run. The Medellín-born star became the first Latina to headline Coachella earlier this year, and her 2023 album Mañana Será Bonito made history as the first all-Spanish-language album by a woman to debut at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. Her 2025 album Tropicoqueta debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard 200, and she announced her latest album, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, in July, extending a run that has established her as the most commercially dominant woman in Latin music. (GS) edged 0.17% higher in the premarket session early Tuesday after reports suggested the bank is considering a plan for David Solomon to step down as CEO and be replaced by Chief Operating Officer John Waldron. According to a report from The Wall Street Journal, which cited people familiar with the matter, the move could come as soon as next year. According to the report, discussions have considered Waldron taking over as CEO around the end of 2027 or in 2028. Waldron currently serves as the bank’s president and COO. Waldron joined Goldman Sachs in 2000. Meanwhile, per current discussions, CEO Solomon is likely to stay on the board as executive chairman for about one to two years after stepping down as CEO, the report noted. The bank has been working over the past year to transition duties related to Waldron’s COO role to its finance chief, Denis Coleman, according to the report. The plan will need to be approved by Goldman’s board, which is likely to happen in the coming months, according to some people familiar with the matter. However, they added that the timing of the leadership transition may be fluid and is subject to change. Waldron’s promotion to CEO would leave the position of president open, although as per the people in the report, it is currently not clear how this will play out. The report said a big part of the problem would be the risk of top executives leaving the firm if they don’t get the title. Reuters cited those executives including the co-heads of the firm’s global banking and markets division Dan Dees and Ashok Varadhan, and Marc Nachmann, global head of asset and wealth management. Before the report on the CEO transition, HSBC raised its price target on Goldman Sachs to $1,007 from $995 and maintained a ‘Hold’ rating on the shares, according to The Fly. The rapper joined the Colombian superstar onstage for a performance of his 2016 hit "One Dance" Drake made a surprise appearance at Karol G‘s concert in Houston on Sunday (Sept. 27), joining the Colombian superstar onstage for a performance of his 2016 hit “One Dance.“ In fan-shot clips from the show, both artists appeared dressed in black, with Drake taking the mic on “One Dance” as Karol G danced beside him before the two moved in close, drawing roars from the crowd. The appearance was the latest in a series of moments between the two stars. Drake attended Karol G’s Toronto show in July, appearing on the venue’s Jumbotron, and had publicly nodded to her on record before their team-up, name-checking her on “New Bestie” from his 2026 project Maid of Honour. The pair then released “Ahí” in August, and the single made an immediate mark on Billboard’s Latin charts. It debuted at No. 1 on Hot Latin Songs — Drake’s fourth leader on the tally — and gave him his first career No. 1 on Hot Latin Rhythm Songs, a chart he had never previously topped. Released in 2016, “One Dance” was a career milestone for Drake. Featuring Nigerian star Wizkid and British singer Kyla, it became his first Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 as a lead artist, spent 10 weeks atop the chart and reigned for years as the most-streamed song in Spotify history. It has since become a staple of his unannounced guest spots, including a surprise set at Vybz Kartel’s Toronto concert last year, where he also performed it. For Karol G, the moment adds to a genre-reshaping run. The Medellín-born star became the first Latina to headline Coachella earlier this year, and her 2023 album Mañana Será Bonito made history as the first all-Spanish-language album by a woman to debut at No. 1 on the Billboard 200. Her 2025 album Tropicoqueta debuted at No. 3 on the Billboard 200, and she announced her latest album, No Me Arrepiento de Sentir Tanto, in July, extending a run that has established her as the most commercially dominant woman in Latin music. Spotify tells Billboard Canada that her streams have grown over the last two weeks, with hits like “On ne change pas” and “Pour que tu m’aimes encore” seeing major gains in her home country.
